olm8ij-g57424-d1e103.summary: Rubric: Question 4, 'On the virtues'. The TEI head labels the item 'Quaestio 1', but the printed text numbers it IV.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e114.summary: States the question: whether something is in humans by nature that is true virtue, or whether habituation turns into true virtue. Damascene (De fide orthodoxa III, 14) says the virtues are truly natural. Against: vice is generated by habituation, so virtues are too. Two assumptions are identified: that humans can attain virtues from natural powers, and that virtues are generated from acts. Four points are announced: whether there is or can be true virtue; whether it comes from acts; whether there is a seed-bed in us that is the principle of virtue; whether natural dispositions can be brought to true virtue by acts.
claims: Damascene holds the virtues to be natural.
Vice is generated by habituation.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e160.summary: Rubric for Article 1: whether true virtues are found in humans.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e167.summary: Sets out a view that political virtues are true virtues, though neither meritorious nor gratuitous. A moral act can have four goodnesses: (1) natural goodness of being; (2) goodness from its object, which is generic or substantial goodness; (3) goodness from good circumstances, chiefly the end; (4) gratuitous goodness, being accepted by God, which requires infused grace and can be absent when the others are present. Since habits are generated from acts with the first three goodnesses, true but not gratuitous virtue can be acquired. A pagan can give alms with the due circumstances and so acquire political virtues.
claims: A moral act may have natural, objective, circumstantial and gratuitous goodness.
Gratuitous goodness requires infused grace and can be absent while the others remain.
On this view, pagans can acquire true political virtues.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e232.summary: Aureol argues against that view: the first three goodnesses do not suffice for true virtue. True virtue cannot be separated from being accepted by God. To be accepted is to be pleasing in God's sight, and God cannot fail to delight in what is truly good, as a secondary object. God has every perfection (Anselm, Monologion 15), and taking pleasure in the truly good is a pure perfection. Aristotle (Ethics I, 8) says virtues are good and delightful in themselves, and an act of pleasure in the good, as resting in it, is of itself a pure perfection.
claims: True virtue cannot be separated from divine acceptance.
God necessarily delights in what is truly good.
Taking pleasure in the true good is a pure perfection.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e290.summary: More arguments. Following Anselm, God would not be perfectly good if he did not render to each its own, so if he did not take pleasure where pleasure is due, he would not be perfectly good. God perfectly hates evil, otherwise he could dispense from the precepts of the first table and make hatred of God good. So with the same necessity he accepts the truly good. A truly good act is pleasing to God, and since such pleasure is the basis of friendship, a truly good act necessarily merits friendship, whether or not glory is given.
claims: God's perfect goodness requires pleasure in what deserves it.
God cannot dispense from the precepts of the first table.
A truly good act necessarily merits God's friendship.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e327.summary: If a truly good act were not pleasing to God, what would be added to make it accepted? If it concerns goodness, the act was not truly good. If not, God would accept the act on grounds other than goodness. Also, whatever is borne to an object is borne with the same necessity to what is necessarily connected with it. True virtues share in the divine goodness, so God, loving his goodness necessarily, necessarily loves true virtues. Objections: God accepts an act only because he wills it, as he accepted Paul despite his demerits. A creature would necessitate God. It is not contradictory for a virtue to be good and not accepted. Aureol says acceptance must be considered in two ways.
claims: True virtues share in divine goodness.
Whoever loves an object necessarily loves what is necessarily connected to it.
Objection: divine acceptance is free, as in Paul's case.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e379.summary: Distinguishes two kinds of divine love. Love of complacency (charity, or friendship) is delight in someone because of the virtue in them. It is necessarily founded on virtue and exists between God and the virtuous, not sinners. Love of desire is efficaciously wishing good to someone, and by it God can freely accept someone in mortal sin and grant them glory. Wishing good comes before taking pleasure. No one can be God's familiar without virtues, and if one has them, God's love of complacency necessarily follows. Against the objection that there can be no friendship between unequal parties, Aureol distinguishes friendship of equality from friendship of analogy, like that between master and servant. Charity between God and the virtuous is of the second kind, so the saints are called friends of God.
claims: God's love of complacency is necessarily founded on the virtue of the beloved.
God's love of desire is free and can extend to those in mortal sin.
Wishing good is prior to taking pleasure.
Friendship between God and humans is a friendship of analogy, not of equality.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e455.summary: Reply to the objection that a creature would necessitate God. A 'reason' mediating between power and act never mediates between the divine will and its act. As an object-reason it may be primary or secondary. No creature can be the primary object of the divine will, but a creature can be a secondary object, in which the will may rest without being necessitated primarily.
claims: No creature is the primary object of the divine will.
Creatures can be secondary objects of the divine will without necessitating it primarily.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e492.summary: The primary necessitating factor is divine goodness, the primary object. From it comes secondary necessity: because God necessarily loves his own goodness, he necessarily takes pleasure in what resembles it.
claims: Divine goodness is the primary necessitating object.
God necessarily takes pleasure in what resembles his goodness.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e505.summary: Reply to the third objection. Impossibility for God regarding creatures arises in three ways: from contradiction of terms, from unfittingness and disorder, or from a change in the divine plan. In the case of sin, will and bad act do not contradict, but the combination includes disorder. God cannot make the will be under a bad act, since that would imply a contradiction in God, who necessarily wills the good and rejects disorder.
claims: Divine impossibility arises from contradiction, from disorder, or from a change of divine plan.
God cannot cause sin, because that would involve a contradiction in God.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e545.summary: Third mode: where the combination of terms implies a change of the divine plan, as the sun not rising. Applied here: it is impossible for God not to take pleasure in the virtuous, from the nature of the thing, since it follows from his primary act of loving his own goodness.
claims: It is impossible for God not to take pleasure in the virtuous.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e563.summary: Answers the claim that a good virtue not being accepted involves no contradiction. Even so, it implies disorder, since acceptance presupposes virtue, and a good not being accepted is disordered. A contradiction in God would follow, so God cannot do it.
claims: Non-acceptance of true virtue implies disorder and so is impossible for God.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e589.summary: Second main argument against acquired true virtue. A truly virtuous act must have all its circumstances, and this is impossible from purely natural powers. Humans reach the precise circumstances only by chance (Ethics II), still less those required by the divine will. Hence the Apostle: 'I am not conscious of anything, yet I am not thereby justified.' Objections: a person might hit all circumstances by chance, and reason can dictate the circumstances God requires.
claims: A truly virtuous act requires all circumstances.
Pure nature reaches the full circumstances only by chance.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e624.summary: Reply to the first objection: an act that hits the circumstances by chance is not virtuous, because it is not chosen. Aristotle (Ethics II, 4) says one who acts by chance is not virtuous, since one does not act firmly and knowingly.
claims: An act hitting the right circumstances by chance is not virtuous.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e640.summary: Reply to the second objection and conclusion. Divine law gives universal precepts, but applying them to particulars requires illumination. Even with intellectual direction, the will can err, and God does not reveal to each person that he directs them in this case. So the full integrity of circumstances cannot be guaranteed. Augustine (City of God V, 19) says unbelievers cannot have true virtues, and Hugh of St Victor says philosophers had only truncated images of virtue. Aureol distinguishes: true virtue simply cannot be acquired naturally, but true virtue in a human mode can.
claims: Applying universal precepts to particulars requires illumination.
True virtue simply taken cannot be acquired naturally.
True virtue in a human mode can be acquired from natural powers.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e706.summary: First of three reasons that virtue in a human mode can be acquired. Otherwise those who laboured to acquire virtue acquired nothing, yet Aristotle's Ethics has nothing base or irrational about virtue. The virtuous person is the rule of what is good, but God alone is good, so his judgment stands. God judges some naturally acquired goods as good in a qualified sense, as Cornelius' prayers and alms were in some way accepted before he believed. So such virtues were true and were taken up toward divine familiarity.
claims: Aristotle and the philosophers grasped some truth about virtue.
God judges naturally acquired virtues good in a qualified sense.
Cornelius' prayers and alms were accepted in some way before his faith.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e766.summary: Second reason: from praise and honour. Honour and praise are due to virtue. Praise declares the virtue present, and honour is like a wage, testifying to goodness. The virtuous are rewarded intrinsically, but among humans only by honour. The saints praise some pagans, so those pagans had true virtue in a qualified sense.
claims: Praise and honour are due to virtue.
Saints praise some pagans, who therefore had qualified true virtue.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e801.summary: Third reason and conclusion that infused virtues are necessary. Goodness is measured by conformity to rules: right reason, a qualified rule, and the divine will, the unqualified rule. From pure nature one can act according to right reason, which discovers but does not confer goodness, but not according to the divine will, which gives goodness simply. So naturally acquired virtue is good only in a qualified sense. Infused virtues are therefore necessary. An agent that can err in infinitely many ways and be right in only one way, and that only by chance, needs a higher agent. As wine offered in a golden cup does not fully please unless the giver is pleasing, an act is not simply good unless its agent is accepted. God's assistance through infused virtues is required.
claims: Right reason is a qualified rule of goodness; the divine will is the unqualified rule.
Natural powers can conform to right reason but not to the divine will.
Infused virtues are necessary for acts that are simply good.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e898.summary: Rubric for Article 2: whether virtues of either kind are generated from acts.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e914.summary: Experience shows that habits are generated from acts: in every art, writing and lyre-playing, in sobriety and other virtues, as Aristotle knew from experience. Bodily strength needs exercise, and in the will bad acts produce bad habits, so good acts produce good habits.
claims: To deny that habits come from acts is to deny experience.
Bad acts generate bad habits and good acts good habits.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e936.summary: Difficulties against generation from acts. Natural acts are no weaker than voluntary acts, yet a stone thrown upward a thousand times is not habituated. Acts of intellect follow habits rather than generate them, since knowledge precedes considering (De anima III). When an effect depends on a cause through an intermediary, it is attributed to the first cause, as heating to the sun rather than its rays, so the habit is caused by object and power, not by the act. A habitual power is in potency first to habit and then to act, so the object reduces it first to habit. Habit is first act, act second act, and habit has causality over act.
claims: A stone is not habituated by repeated throwing.
Knowledge precedes the act of considering.
An effect through an intermediary is attributed to the first cause.
Habit is first act and prior in nature to the second act.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1007.summary: Further difficulties specific to the will. A form does not act on its subject, and both habit and act are qualities in the will. One distinct species does not produce another in the same genus. There is no circle of production between equivocal causes, since the equivocal cause is nobler. A single act does not produce a habit, by experience, and many acts do not exist together. Aureol suggests it would be more reasonable to say that power and object generate both habit and act, the habit first in order of nature, as an object impresses species and act together but species first. He allows that one can also hold that the act causes the habit and answer the objections.
claims: A form does not act on its own subject.
Disparate species do not produce one another.
Neither one act nor a sum of acts produces a habit.
Perhaps object and power produce both habit and act, the habit first in nature.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1092.summary: Replies to the objections. Acts do change natural powers: sight that is kept in darkness without exercise is altered. Gravity suffices for the stone's motion and is not increased or decreased by contrary motion. Sight needs more media, as do intellect and will. Some acts presuppose a habit as cause, as knowledge causes scientific acts. Others, such as apprehending terms, generate the habit of principles. So some acts precede habits and some follow them.
claims: Exercise or lack of it alters natural powers such as sight.
Some acts generate habits and others proceed from them.
The habit of principles is generated by apprehending terms.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1138.summary: Further on knowledge. If knowledge is a truth-telling habit for conclusions, it precedes the truth-telling act. If it comes from acts, one says it gives the ability to act scientifically, not that one could not act from principles without it.
claims: Knowledge as a truth-telling habit precedes the truth-telling act.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1156.summary: Reply to the argument from the first cause. It holds where the first cause is not indeterminate between opposite effects. Where it is indeterminate, the effect must be traced to the second cause, as intemperance is determined by acts. Alternatively, object and power contain the habit virtually in a certain order.
claims: When the first cause is indeterminate, the effect is attributed to the determining second cause.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1176.summary: Reply on the order of habit and act. The habit is prior, but it is the cause of subsequent acts, not of the first acts. Although acts are of the same kind, some circumstance explains why the habit acts in later acts and not in the first.
claims: The habit causes subsequent acts, not the first acts that generate it.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1192.summary: Reply to the claim that a form cannot act on its subject. A form in a resting state perhaps cannot act, but Aureol sees nothing unfitting in a form acting while formally present, as a sun's ray, present subjectively, produces heat.
claims: A form can act while present in its subject.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1209.summary: Further replies. One species can generate another, as a she-ass and horse produce a mule. On circularity: the object might produce the act through the habit, or the habit causes some circumstances in the act, not its substance. On many acts: each act leaves something in the power, and the last completes the habit by adding the final degree. The habit is caused by the object, simultaneously in time with the act but prior in nature.
claims: One species can generate another.
The habit causes circumstances of the act, not its substance.
Earlier acts each contribute to the habit, and the last completes it.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1253.summary: Turns to whether what is in us by nature is true virtue. This can be understood in two ways. One is whether virtues are in us formally or potentially. This is not the question's sense: Aristotle (Ethics II, 5) says they are in us potentially and become actual by exercise, against Plato, for whom acts would only remove impediments. Plato's view would make opposite habits coexist. So, with Aristotle, virtues are in us in potency and completed by acts.
claims: Virtues are in us potentially and become actual through exercise.
The Platonic view would imply that opposite habits coexist.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1284.summary: Second sense: natural dispositions found more in some than others, as some are naturally liberal, brave or temperate. Are they true virtues? Arguments for yes: what is truly praiseworthy seems true virtue, and we praise the naturally humble. Virtue is a disposition toward acts that are well or badly done, and such dispositions are. Virtue's definition fits them: it perfects its possessor and makes their work good, eliciting acts with the due circumstances.
claims: Some people are naturally inclined to particular virtues.
Arguments: natural dispositions are praiseworthy and fit the definition of virtue.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1326.summary: More arguments for natural virtue. Where there is more and less, there is also an equal, so in some people the natural disposition will match reason, and that will be true virtue. Natural prudence is so necessary that no one becomes prudent by acquisition without it, and the same goes for other virtues: no one becomes gentle without an inclination to it.
claims: Where there is more and less, there is also an equal.
Acquired prudence presupposes natural prudence.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1357.summary: Aureol's argument that natural dispositions are not true virtues. A disposition that makes acts pleasant or unpleasant only as acts, not as good according to reason, is not true virtue. Natural dispositions are like this.
claims: A disposition making acts pleasant only as acts, not as rationally good, is not true virtue.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1375.summary: Proof of the argument. Virtue consists in delighting in some acts and being saddened by others (Ethics II, against the Stoics), and makes right choice (Ethics VI). From delight and sadness come facility, firmness and promptness. A disposition that delights in an act only as an act will sometimes exceed, as one who delights in giving as such gives too much or to the wrong person. Virtue lies in the mean. The gentle by temperament avoid anger not because it is against reason but because it does not please them. Such delight comes from bodily complexion, which regards acts as acts, as the naturally liberal person pours themselves out in giving.
claims: Virtue consists in rightly ordered delight and sadness.
From delight and sadness come facility, firmness and promptness.
Natural dispositions, rooted in complexion, delight in acts as such and so sometimes exceed the mean.
Virtue consists in the mean of reason.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1465.summary: Reply to the first argument. Not everything praiseworthy is virtue: shame is praiseworthy but not a virtue. Alternatively, such dispositions are praiseworthy as signs of nobility of soul or complexion, since those so inclined are more easily brought to virtue.
claims: Shame is praiseworthy but not a virtue.
Natural dispositions are praised as signs and as easier paths to virtue.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1487.summary: Replies to the other arguments. Natural dispositions do not make the work good, because they lack the mean of reason, and if they hit the mean it is not from their nature. They do not formally regard well and ill, since they regard acts for their own sake. They are in the second species of quality, while their passions are in the third. Shame is a passion, praiseworthy because it restrains youth. The definition of virtue does not fit, since a passion never aims at the mean of reason. The gentle person, in not getting angry, does not seek the mean but delights in the act itself.
claims: Natural dispositions lack the mean of reason.
Natural dispositions are in the second species of quality; their passions in the third.
Passions never aim at the mean of reason.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1539.summary: Reply to the argument from 'more, less and equal'. If a natural disposition hits the mean, it is by chance, since virtue's object is the mean of reason while the disposition's object is the act itself. On natural prudence: it disposes to prudence but is not prudence. Natural industry concerns acts in any matter, good or bad, while the virtue of prudence concerns a determinate matter and the good end.
claims: A natural disposition hits the mean only by chance.
Natural industry is indifferent; prudence is directed to the good.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1581.summary: Further replies. It is false that no one acquires true virtue without a natural disposition, though it is harder without one. Why is there no natural disposition to the mean itself? Because such dispositions arise from complexion. Complexion can match an act but cannot produce the mean of reason, which varies by matter while complexion stays the same. God gave animals what they need to act perfectly, since their good is in the act simply, like a horse's running well. In humans the good lies in the mean of reason, which cannot be connatural to complexion. This settles the third point, on which the solution chiefly depends.
claims: True virtue can be acquired without natural disposition, though with more difficulty.
Complexion cannot produce the mean of reason, which varies with matter.
Animals' good lies in the act simply; humans' in the mean of reason.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1625.summary: Last point: can a natural disposition pass into true virtue? Arguments for yes. Things sharing a common quality pass into each other more easily, and the naturally disposed become virtuous more easily. Either the disposition passes into virtue or there would be two liberalities. Extremes pass into the mean. Averroes says there is no alteration in virtues. As health results from balance of humours, virtue results from balance of dispositions. And Aristotle says that a passion becomes virtue by a change in reason alone.
claims: Arguments: natural dispositions ease the acquisition of virtue and might become it.
Virtue might result from balancing dispositions, as health from balancing humours.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1667.summary: Aureol's two conclusions: a natural disposition never passes into true virtue, but it disposes to it. First: virtues with different objects are not the same. The natural disposition has the act itself as object, true virtue the good of reason, so one cannot become the other without a change of species. However much reason dictates, it never inclines the natural disposition to the mean. Second: what removes an impediment disposes to acquiring virtue. One who delights in giving is less impeded than one who is saddened by it. So the naturally proud can scarcely become humble, and humble acts will sometimes displease them.
claims: A natural disposition never becomes true virtue, since their objects differ.
A natural disposition removes impediments and so disposes to virtue.
The naturally proud can scarcely become humble.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1729.summary: Reply to the first argument. An opposite natural disposition never remains with the opposed virtue, but a conforming one can. The acquired virtue moderates the natural disposition, and the natural disposition helps the acquired virtue.
claims: An opposite natural disposition does not coexist with the contrary virtue.
Conforming natural and acquired dispositions help each other.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1742.summary: Concedes that there can be two habits, one natural and one acquired, and that this is helpful: the brave person who is angry is helped in bravery and strikes harder.
claims: A natural and an acquired habit can coexist and cooperate.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1753.summary: More replies. Virtue lies in the mean of reason, while natural extremes approach only a mean in the thing. No complexion has a mean in the thing, and extremes of passion are not virtuous. Someone angry for five days could be good and virtuous in some case. On Averroes: the disposition to the mean of reason lies between natural dispositions, but the mean itself is not altered when virtue is acquired. On health: the analogy fails, because natural virtue is in the first species of quality and disposition in the second.
claims: Virtue lies in the mean of reason, not the mean in the thing.
Extremes of passion are not virtuous.
The analogy between virtue and health fails.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1799.summary: Final reply, to Damascene: virtues are natural and common to humans with respect to the mean of reason, through which they are acquired, but not as virtues themselves.
claims: Damascene's natural virtues are natural only as regards the mean of reason by which virtues are acquired.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1824.summary: Rubric for Article 3: whether the act of hope is formally desiring.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1831.summary: Argument for yes: every act of will toward the good is desire or delight, and hope tends toward an absent good, so it is desire. Against: desiring belongs to the concupiscible, hoping to the irascible. First opinion: hoping is formally believing, a belief about a particular supernatural truth, namely that one will be saved.
claims: Every act of will toward the good is desire or delight.
Desiring is concupiscible; hoping is irascible.
On the first opinion, hope is a kind of belief.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1868.summary: Second opinion: hoping is not believing but desiring. Desire of friendship, by which we desire every good, is charity's act. Desire of concupiscence, by which one desires good for oneself, such as beatitude, is hope's act.
claims: On the second opinion, hope is desire of concupiscence for one's own beatitude.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1900.summary: Third opinion, combining the first two: hoping includes both desiring beatitude for oneself and believing it possible and attainable.
claims: On the third opinion, hope includes desire and belief.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1913.summary: Fourth opinion, like the third but distinguishing differently: absolute desire belongs to charity, while desiring goods for oneself, such as beatitude, is concupiscence, which is the same as hoping.
claims: On the fourth opinion, desiring beatitude for oneself is hoping.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1929.summary: First proposition: all four opinions are to be rejected (the print reads 'relativi', evidently for 'reiciendi'). First, hoping is not formally believing. Believing is an act of intellect, hoping of appetite, as the hopeful are called spirited and magnanimous, traits placed in appetite. Rhetoric II, 5 says hope produces operations, which an intellectual act does not do immediately. The first opinion commits the fallacy of the consequent: the hopeful believe, but hope adds a movement of will that conforms to belief.
claims: All four opinions are to be rejected.
Hope is an act of appetite, not of intellect.
Hope adds to belief a movement of will conformed to it.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e1971.summary: Second, hoping is not desiring. Desiring is common to the hopeful and the despairing: one who despairs of beatitude can desire it intensely. If one says desire in the despairing comes with sorrow and in the hopeful with joy, then hope would be rejoicing, which concerns present good. Desire is concupiscible and hope irascible, and they use different bodily instruments: the irascible acts through the hot and dry, so the choleric are hopeful, while the concupiscible uses the hot and moist, so the sanguine desire. Third, hoping is not believing and desiring together, since hoping is a simple act of a simple power and does not include acts of different powers.
claims: Desire is common to the hopeful and the despairing.
The irascible works through the hot and dry; the concupiscible through the hot and moist.
Hope is a simple act and cannot combine acts of different powers.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e2041.summary: Second proposition: hoping is formally a movement of the will, a spiritual rising toward an arduous good, or a spiritual and intentional reaching of it. Proofs. (1) Every irascible act is a spiritual rising, as shown for anger (not formally desire for revenge), daring (rising against evil) and despair (falling from a good, as a desired prebend). Without this the irascible and concupiscible would not differ. The physiology of the hot and dry fits: the hot are hopeful, the cold and moist despairing and fearful. Both powers are rooted in the heart but use different instruments. In the will, they are distinct immaterial powers, or at least distinct acts. Bodily changes such as blood rising round the heart are effects of the spiritual act, not anger itself. (2) The object's formal aspect determines the act: good attracts, but arduous good calls for rising. Arduousness is not the formal aspect of the object but a necessary concomitant condition, the difficulty of acquiring it, like the nearness of fire to tow. (3) The intellect's firm judgment that the arduous good can be reached corresponds to a like act in appetite, hence 'hope is expectation of a future arduous good'. Corollary: the five irascible passions: anger (present evil, rising), daring (future evil, rising), fear (future evil, falling), hope (future good, rising), despair (future good, falling).
claims: Hoping is formally a spiritual rising of the will toward an arduous good.
Every irascible act is a spiritual rising or falling regarding an arduous object.
Bodily changes are effects of the spiritual irascible act, not the act itself.
Arduousness is a concomitant condition of the object, the difficulty of attaining it, not its formal aspect.
There are exactly five irascible passions: anger, daring, fear, hope and despair.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e2373.summary: Adds that there can be no falling with respect to a present good, since it is already possessed, just as with present evil. This completes the sufficiency of the five irascible passions.
claims: No irascible falling concerns a present good.
The five irascible passions are complete.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e2385.summary: Reply to the opening argument: it commits the fallacy of the consequent, since not every act of will toward the good, absolute or arduous, is desire or delight.
claims: Not every act of will toward the good is desire or delight.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e2406.summary: Rubric for Article 4: whether hope is a theological virtue.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e2413.summary: Argument for no: hope does not have God as its object as it has him as its end. One does not hope for God but for beatitude.
claims: One hopes for beatitude rather than for God.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e2424.summary: Argument in the opposite direction: the Apostle (1 Corinthians 13) lists hope among the theological virtues. Aureol's main proposition: neither beatitude nor anything created is the object of hope. God under the aspect of deity is. He rejects the view that created beatitude is the immediate object, which appeals to delight in the vision of God following hope. Against it: by common teaching, theological virtues have God as immediate object, other virtues something created. Latria is a moral virtue with God as mediate object, through the creature offered, so if hope had God only mediately it would be moral, not theological.
claims: God under the aspect of deity is the object of hope.
Theological virtues have God as immediate object.
Latria has God only as mediate object and is therefore a moral virtue.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e2482.summary: Third argument. What can be separated from the act on the object's side does not belong to its formal aspect. One can hope in God absolutely, apart from anything created, as one trusts in a king without counting on any specific aid. When something created enters, such as beatitude or victory, it is material, not formal. Hence 'Blessed are all who hope in the Lord.'
claims: What is separable from the act is not the formal aspect of its object.
One can hope in God absolutely, without any created object.
Created goods hoped for are only material objects of hope.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e2528.summary: Fourth argument. What I hope for is the material object, and that in which I hope is the formal object, as with faith, where what is believed differs from that by which one believes. God is the one in whom we hope, the formal object. Beatitude is what we hope to obtain, the material object. One does not hope in beatitude but in God.
claims: What is hoped for is the material object; that in which one hopes is the formal object.
God is the formal object of hope; beatitude its material object.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e2567.summary: Confirmation and first conclusions. What varies hope is the formal object, the one in whom one hopes: people hoping for the same thing from different sources (health from a physician or from God) have different hopes. So with knowledge: the conclusion is material, the principle formal. The objection about delight is answered: 'tentio' and the delight of friendship succeed hope and concern the divine good immediately. Conclusion: hope is a virtue, the most noble, because it raises one to God as its formal object. Its act is praiseworthy, as despair is blameworthy, and lies in the mean between presumption and despair. Against those who deny it is most properly a virtue: only charity is perhaps virtue in the superabundant sense.
claims: The source in which one hopes, not what is hoped for, specifies hope.
Tentio and delight of friendship succeed hope.
Hope is a most noble virtue, raising one toward God.
Hope lies in the mean between presumption and despair.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e2645.summary: Conclusion (numbered 'fourth' in the print, in the place of a second): hope is an infused virtue and a gift of God. Objection: if no hope could be acquired, we could know that we have an infused virtue. Reply: a habit of hoping in God can be acquired from acts, but the fitting habit with all its circumstances must be infused.
claims: Hope proper is an infused virtue.
An acquired habit of hoping in God is possible, but complete hope requires infusion.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e2669.summary: Third conclusion: hope is a theological virtue, since its act tends directly toward God under the aspect of deity, holding him intentionally. Objection: being a mean between two vices is proper to moral virtues, as we cannot love or believe in God too much. Reply: not every mean between vices makes a moral virtue, as justice is moral without being a mean between two vices. Alternatively, there is a mean in theological virtues: one can believe superstitiously or unbelievingly, and hope presumptuously or despairingly.
claims: Hope is a theological virtue because it tends directly to God.
Being a mean between vices does not make a virtue moral.
Theological virtues can also have a mean.

olm8ij-g57424-d1e2713.summary: Fourth conclusion: hope can be unformed, like faith. Objection: one who hopes for glory without grace presumes. Reply: hope requires only rising toward God with due circumstances, trusting in mercy or justice. A person in mortal sin can hope that God will forgive and give grace and so glory. Hoping for glory while remaining in sin would be presumption. Doubt: if the object of hope is an arduous good, how is God its object? Reply: arduousness is a condition of the material object, as enigma is for faith. A proposition indifferent from its terms is referred to God, who cannot deceive, as the formal object. So in hope I hope for glory materially and turn to God, who can give it in mercy, formally. This answers the opening argument.
claims: Hope can exist unformed, without charity.
Hope for glory while remaining in sin is presumption.
Arduousness is a condition of hope's material object, not its formal object.
Glory is hoped for materially; God is hoped in formally.

olm8ij-g57424-Dd1e153.summary: Article 1 asks whether there are true virtues in humans, and in particular whether naturally acquired, political virtues are true virtues. A first view distinguishes four goodnesses of a moral act (natural, from the object, from circumstances, gratuitous). It holds that pagans can acquire true though non-gratuitous virtue. Aureol objects that true virtue cannot be separated from divine acceptance, since God necessarily takes pleasure in the truly good, which shares in his goodness. He distinguishes God's free love of desire, by which he can accept even sinners, from his necessary love of complacency. The latter is founded on virtue and is a friendship of analogy, not equality. Creatures are secondary objects of the divine will and do not necessitate it primarily. Non-acceptance of true virtue would be a disorder implying contradiction in God. Further, true virtue requires all circumstances, which pure nature reaches only by chance, since applying universal law to particulars requires illumination. Aureol concludes that true virtue simply cannot be acquired naturally, though true virtue in a human mode can. The arguments are Aristotle's sound ethics, God's qualified acceptance of Cornelius' alms, and the honour saints give to pagans. Right reason is a qualified rule of goodness, the divine will the unqualified one, so infused virtues are necessary for simply good acts.
claims: True virtue simply taken is inseparable from divine acceptance.
God's love of complacency necessarily rests on virtue; his love of desire is free.
God cannot fail to take pleasure in the truly virtuous.
True virtue simply cannot be acquired from natural powers; virtue in a human mode can.
Right reason is a qualified rule of goodness, the divine will the unqualified rule.
Infused virtues are necessary for simply good acts.

olm8ij-g57424-Dd1e891.summary: Article 2 asks whether virtues are generated from acts, and goes on to the natural seed-bed of virtue and whether it can become virtue. Experience shows that habits come from acts. Aureol states strong objections: the stone is not habituated, knowledge precedes considering, effects are attributed to the first cause, a form does not act on its subject, and neither one act nor many produce a habit. He finds it reasonable that object and power produce habit and act together, the habit prior in nature, but shows that generation from acts can also be defended. Exercise alters powers, some acts generate habits (as of principles), the last act completes what earlier ones began, and habit causes later acts' circumstances. Natural virtues in the Aristotelian sense are in us in potency and completed by exercise, against Plato. Natural dispositions, such as being naturally liberal or gentle, are not true virtues. Rooted in complexion, they delight in acts as acts and not as the mean of reason, so they sometimes exceed and hit the mean only by chance. They are praised only as signs of a noble nature, and are in the second species of quality. Such a disposition never passes into true virtue, since its object differs, but it disposes to virtue by removing impediments. A conforming natural disposition can coexist with and assist acquired virtue. Damascene's 'natural virtues' are natural only as to the mean of reason through which virtue is acquired.
claims: Habits are generated from acts, as experience shows.
Habit and act may be produced by object and power together, the habit prior in nature.
Virtues are in us potentially and completed by exercise.
Natural dispositions are not true virtues because they regard acts as such, not the mean of reason.
A natural disposition never becomes true virtue but disposes to it by removing impediments.
Complexion cannot produce the mean of reason, which varies with matter.

olm8ij-g57424-Dd1e1817.summary: Article 3 asks whether the act of hope is formally desiring. Aureol reviews four opinions: hope is believing; hope is desire of concupiscence; hope combines desire and belief; desiring good for oneself is hoping. He rejects all four. Hope is an act of appetite, not intellect, since it produces operations and makes one spirited. It is not desire, since the despairing can desire as much as the hopeful, and desire is concupiscible while hope is irascible. Nor is it a combination, since it is a simple act of a simple power. His thesis: hoping is formally a spiritual rising (assurrectio) of the will toward an arduous good, an intentional reaching of it. This follows from the general nature of irascible acts as rising or falling, from the formal aspect of the arduous object, and from the will's correspondence to the intellect's firm judgment of attainability. Bodily changes are effects, not essence. Arduousness, the difficulty of attaining, is a concomitant condition of the object rather than its formal aspect. A corollary derives exactly five irascible passions: anger, daring, fear, hope and despair.
claims: Hope is neither believing, nor desiring, nor their combination.
Hoping is formally a spiritual rising of the will toward an arduous good.
Arduousness is a concomitant condition of the object, not its formal aspect.
There are exactly five irascible passions: anger, daring, fear, hope, despair.

olm8ij-g57424-Dd1e2399.summary: Article 4 asks whether hope is a theological virtue. Against the view that its immediate object is created beatitude, Aureol argues that God under the aspect of deity is its object. Theological virtues have God as immediate object, while latria, which has God only through a creature offered, is moral. One can hope in God absolutely, apart from any creature. The distinction between what is hoped for (beatitude, the material object) and that in which one hopes (God, the formal object) parallels faith and knowledge. It is confirmed by the fact that hopes are specified by their source. He concludes that hope is a most noble virtue, the mean between presumption and despair. It is infused, though an imperfect acquired habit of hoping in God is possible. It is theological, since a mean between vices does not make a virtue moral. It can be unformed, so a sinner may hope for forgiveness and glory, while hoping for glory while remaining in sin is presumption. The arduousness of hope's object belongs to its material object, as enigma does to faith's.
claims: God under the aspect of deity is the formal object of hope; beatitude its material object.
Hope is a most noble virtue, a mean between presumption and despair.
Hope proper is infused.
Hope is a theological virtue.
Hope can exist unformed.

olm8ij-g57424.summary: Question 4 of Aureol's commentary on Book III, Distinction 23 (on the virtues) asks whether anything in humans by nature is true virtue, or whether habituation passes into true virtue. Article 1 argues that true virtue simply taken requires divine acceptance, since God necessarily delights in true goodness through his love of complacency. Pure nature cannot secure the integrity of circumstances, so infused virtues are necessary. Yet philosophers and pagans can acquire true virtue in a human mode, conformed to right reason. Article 2 defends the generation of habits from acts against serious objections. It holds that virtues are in us potentially, not as Platonic latent forms, and that natural, complexion-based dispositions are not virtues. They delight in acts as such rather than in the mean of reason, never become virtue, but dispose to it. Articles 3 and 4 turn to hope. Its act is formally neither belief nor desire but a spiritual rising of the will toward an arduous good, the basis of a derivation of the five irascible passions. It is an infused, theological virtue whose formal object is God and whose material object is beatitude, and it can exist unformed.
claims: True virtue simply taken requires divine acceptance and infused virtue; virtue in a human mode can be naturally acquired.
Natural, complexion-based dispositions are not virtues and never become virtues, though they dispose to them.
Hope is formally a spiritual rising toward an arduous good.
Hope is an infused theological virtue with God as its formal object.
